description_full: ABB Ltd provides electrification, motion, and automation solutions and products for customers in utilities, industry and transport, and infrastructure in Europe, the Americas, Asia, the Middle East, and Africa. The company operates through Electrification, Motion, and Automation segments. Its Electrification segment offers renewable power solutions, modular substation packages, distribution automation products, switchboards and panelboards, switchgears, UPS solutions, circuit breakers, measuring and sensing devices, control products, wiring accessories, enclosures and cabling systems, and intelligent home and building solutions. The company's Motion segment designs, manufactures, and sells drives, motors, generators, and traction converters that are driving the low-carbon future for industries, cities, infrastructure, and transportation. The company's Automation segment offers industry-specific, integrated automation, electrification and digital solutions, as well as lifecycle services for the process, hybrid and marine industries. This segment also provides control technologies; process, machine and factory automation; industrial software; advanced analytics; sensing and measurement technology; and marine propulsion systems; services such as remote monitoring, preventive maintenance, asset performance management, emission monitoring and cybersecurity. It serves oil, gas, renewables, chemicals, mining, metals, cement, pulp and paper, pharmaceuticals, battery manufacturing, food and beverage, space, power generation, water, marine, and ports industries. The company was founded in 1883 and is headquartered in Zurich, Switzerland.

culture_narrative: Employs approximately 115K people. Revenue per employee of $280K ranks in the below the sector median among Industrials peers. Each employee generates $31K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $893 per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 18× revenue per employee (reasonable relative to workforce productivity).
financial_summary: ABB Ltd. is a large-cap industrials business with a $151.6B market cap on $32.2B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +7% over the past three years and -3% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.
Returns on capital run at 17% against a 9% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it, with gross margins sitting at 30%.

The business throws off $3.5B in free cash flow — roughly 11 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.15× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 19× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield is only 2.0%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sector_headwinds.text: Price sits 405% above estimated fair value — no margin of safety left, and the cushion against estimate error has been bid away (confirmed by 2 other valuation measures)
Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Volatile returns on capital suggest the moat is narrower than a snapshot ROIC implies
Industrials sector lagging the market significantly, underperforming by 6% over 3 months
Cyclicality and capital intensity — order books turn on a dime, and the heavy fixed cost base that creates the moat also magnifies the downturn.
Supply chain reshoring costs and labour shortages — onshoring mandates raise capex requirements while a shrinking skilled-labour pool inflates operating costs.
Tariff and trade-policy exposure — industrial exporters sit squarely in the crosshairs of protectionist policy, and retaliatory tariffs can close markets without warning.

sector_tailwinds: Piotroski score 7/9 — financials improving across profitability, leverage and efficiency
Altman Z comfortably in the safe zone — a fortress balance sheet on this measure
20 consecutive years of dividend payments — an operating record that makes the dividend claim credible
Healthy payout ratio leaves room for both dividend growth and reinvestment

sect: Its 15% operating margin runs 6pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.36x).
It accounts for 0.8% of sector revenue and 1.1% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+11.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 548 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 39% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 18% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 24% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 35% and a beta of 1.02, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 1.53 vs 5y 1.02), so read it loosely.
About $18.6M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 41% in the 2020 crash, 33% in the 2022 bear market and 72% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $16.58 (margin of safety -405%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 30%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $12.34 to $22.75 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Industrials peers: P/E 30.3 vs 24.1, EV/EBITDA 82.6 vs 13.4 and P/FCF 43.1 vs 22.9 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 177% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.3% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 0.8% (vs the 8% bar).
The 6 covering analysts target $94.71 on average, 13% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 17% clears the cost of capital of 9.4% by 7pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.59).
It runs a 30% gross margin and converts 11% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.15x.
ROE of 28% is amplified by 3.1x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 4.1% of revenue on R&D and 0.3% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.4x net debt to EBITDA ($5.8B of cash against $7.8B of debt), with interest covered 19.5x.
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 5.3, in the safe zone).
growth: Revenue has compounded at 7.2% over 3 years, 3.1% over 5 years and -2.6% over 10 years, so growth is accelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 6% of profits supports about 0.9% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 10.3% a year over five years.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.05 (orders outpacing sales), a backlog worth 67% of annual revenue and deferred revenue up 25%.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.0x, 2.4% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 14, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.0%), and institutions hold 0%.
Shareholder yield is a modest 2.0% (0.8% in buybacks and 1.4% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 2.9% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 20 consecutive years.
people: With about 115,300 employees, each generates about $280K of revenue, 0.8x the Industrials median.
That works out to $31K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.1M (18x revenue per employee).
